title: No homomorphisms from unipotent groups to groups of multiplicative type
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All groups below are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$; subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness are as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] and [def-weil-connected-scheme]. A group scheme $V$ is called unipotent if after extension to an algebraic closure [def-weil-algebraic-closure] it admits a closed immersion into the group of upper triangular matrices with every diagonal entry $1$. For smooth $V$ this is equivalent to every geometric point being a unipotent matrix in a faithful representation, meaning $(u-I)^N=0$ for some $N\geq1$. A group scheme $D$ is of multiplicative type if after extension to an algebraic closure it is isomorphic to a closed subgroup of $(\mathbf G_m)^r$ for some $r\geq0$, with $\mathbf G_m$ as in [def-sc-gm-ga]. Unipotence and multiplicative type are preserved by, and can be tested after, any field extension. Every group-scheme homomorphism $f:V\to D$ from a unipotent group scheme $V$ to a group scheme $D$ of multiplicative type is trivial: for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and $v\in V(A)$ one has $f_A(v)=1$. There is no smoothness or connectedness hypothesis on $V$ or $D$.

source.place: Corollary 14.18(a), printed p.284; Corollary 14.9 and Corollary 14.12, printed pp.282–283, for field-extension invariance and smooth geometric-point comparison; Definition 12.17 and Theorem 12.23, printed pp.236,240, for multiplicative type under scalar extension.

proof.text: First verify the field-extension assertion for both geometric embedding conditions. Let $K/k$ be any field extension, let $F=\bar k$, and choose an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $K$. By [lem-weil-pbc-algebraic-extension-embeds-algebraically-closed], the inclusion $k\to\Omega$ extends to $F\to\Omega$. The two ways of extending a group from $k$ to $\Omega$ agree: [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] identifies their coordinates by $(B\otimes_k F)\otimes_F\Omega\simeq B\otimes_k\Omega\simeq(B\otimes_k K)\otimes_K\Omega$. For each fixed $n\geq1$, a closed embedding into $\mathcal U_{n,F}$ exists if and only if one exists after extension to $\Omega$, by [lem-sfb-algclosed-group-embedding-existence-descent]. The same argument applies to $\mathbf G_{m,F}^r$ for each $r\geq0$. The targets have polynomial, respectively Laurent polynomial, coordinate presentations, so are affine of finite type, including the trivial target at $r=0$. Since $\Omega$ is an algebraic closure of $K$, existence over $\Omega$ is exactly the definition for the original group over $K$. Thus unipotence and multiplicative type are both preserved and reflected by $K/k$.

source.place: Corollary 14.9, p.282; Definition 12.17, p.236. Agent assembly from finite-presentation existence descent.

proof.text: For the smooth comparison, suppose $V$ is smooth and every geometric point is unipotent in a supplied faithful representation. Apply [lem-sfb-geometric-unipotence-unitriangular-embedding] to obtain a closed embedding into $\mathcal U_n$ over $k$, hence over $\bar k$, proving geometric unipotence. Conversely, a unitriangular closed embedding $i:V_{\bar k}\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_{n,\bar k}$ has $(i(u)-I)^n=0$ for every $u\in V(\bar k)$: the product of $n$ strictly upper triangular matrices is zero. Given any other faithful representation $\rho$ of $V$, extend it to $\bar k$ and apply [lem-sfb-rational-representation-unipotent-point] with faithful representation $i$ and representation $\rho_{\bar k}$. Every $\rho(u)$ is unipotent. In particular a faithful geometric representation exists (namely $i$), and whenever a faithful representation is specified the criterion agrees with it. Only the converse from geometric points invoked smoothness.

Now work over $F=\bar k$. Choose the defining closed embeddings $i:V_F\hookrightarrow\mathcal U_{n,F}$ and $j:D_F\hookrightarrow\mathbf G_{m,F}^r$. For each coordinate $a=1,\ldots,r$, the composite $\chi_a=\operatorname{pr}_a\circ j\circ f_F:V_F\to\mathbf G_m=\operatorname{GL}_1$ is a rational representation on $F$. Apply [lem-sfb-unitriangular-subgroup-rational-fixed-vector] with $d=1$ to obtain $v_a\ne0$ fixed over every $F$-algebra $A$. The equation $\chi_{a,A}(u)v_a=v_a$ implies $\chi_{a,A}(u)=1$, since $v_a$ is a nonzero scalar of the field and remains invertible in $A$. Thus $j_A(f_{F,A}(u))=(1,\ldots,1)=j_A(1)$ for every $A,u$. A closed immersion is injective on $A$-points: its coordinate map is surjective, so two algebra maps agreeing after it agree everywhere [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Consequently $f_F$ is the identity-valued morphism. This also covers $r=0$, since the target product then has one point over every $A$.

source.place: The representation argument of Proposition 14.16 and Corollary 14.18(a), p.284; Theorem 14.5, pp.281–282.

proof.text: Descend equality of the two morphisms, not just equality on geometric points. Write $B=k[V]$ and $C=k[D]$. By [def-weil-affine-spectrum] it suffices to show that $f^*:C\to B$ is the same as the identity-valued map $c\mapsto\epsilon_D(c)1_B$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], step 3 gives $(f^*(c)-\epsilon_D(c)1_B)\otimes1=0$ in $B\otimes_k F$ for every $c$. The map $B\to B\otimes_k F$ is injective: choose a $k$-linear functional $\lambda:F\to k$ with $\lambda(1)=1$ by extending $1$ to a basis; $1_B\otimes\lambda$ is a left inverse. Hence $f^*(c)=\epsilon_D(c)1_B$. Evaluating this equality on any $k$-algebra $A$ proves $f_A(v)=1$ for every $v\in V(A)$. None of these steps imposed smoothness or connectedness on either group.

source.place: Corollary 14.18(a), p.284, with explicit faithful field-extension detection on affine coordinates.
